chapters.title: Chapter 3: Switching Costs and Network Effects

lessons.title: Network Effects: Exchanges, Depositories, Payments, and Marketplaces

body.text: Most products lose value as more people use them: crowded roads, busy restaurants, oversubscribed IPOs. A network gains value with every new user. That reversal is one of the most powerful moats in business.

markDefs.definition: When a product or service becomes more valuable to each user as more people use it. It creates a self-reinforcing loop: more users attract more users.

children.text: A
network effect

exists when each additional user makes the product more useful for everyone else. Traders go to the exchange with the most traders. Jobseekers go to the job site with the most recruiters, and recruiters go where the jobseekers are. Once a network is clearly ahead, the gap tends to widen on its own, and a rival with a better product and more money can still fail to catch up.
Why Networks Get Stronger as They Grow
The value of a network comes from the connections it makes possible. Every new user can connect with every existing one, so possible connections grow much faster than the number of users.

body.caption: n = number of users. This is the idea behind Metcalfe's law, which says network value grows roughly with the square of users.

body.title: Count the Connections
body.prompt: A new B2B marketplace has 50 members, and any member can trade with any other. How many possible trading connections exist?
body.explanation: Connections = 50 × 49 ÷ 2 = 1,225. Doubling to 100 members gives 4,950 connections, roughly four times as many. That is why the leading network pulls further ahead as it grows.

children.text: Metcalfe's law is a useful intuition, not a valuation formula. In practice, most users only interact with a small part of any network. A food delivery customer in Pune gets no value from a restaurant in Guwahati. Real network value depends on relevant connections, which is why many network effects are local, not national.
Treat the formula as a reminder that networks can grow in value faster than they grow in users, not as a way to put a price on a company.
Four Kinds of Network Effects in Indian Markets

body.caption: How network effects work in listed Indian businesses

cells: Buyers and sellers go where the most other buyers and sellers already trade, because prices are tighter and orders fill faster
MCX in commodity derivatives; stock exchanges in equity derivatives
Two different groups attract each other: more of one side brings more of the other
Info Edge's Naukri (recruiters and jobseekers); IndiaMART (business buyers and suppliers)
Intermediaries and institutions connect to shared infrastructure, making it the default for new participants
CDSL, where brokers acting as depository participants open demat accounts for their clients
More customers support more delivery partners and restaurants in a city, which improves speed and choice, attracting more customers
Eternal (Zomato) and Swiggy in food delivery and quick commerce

children.text: Liquidity: Why Traders Crowd onto One Exchange

markDefs.definition: The gap between the highest price a buyer will pay and the lowest price a seller will accept. Narrower spreads mean lower hidden trading costs.

children.text: On an exchange, liquidity is the product. A trader wants the narrowest
bid-ask spread

and the fastest fills, and that only exists where other traders already are. A new exchange can offer lower fees, but if its order book is thin, traders pay more through wider spreads than they save on fees. That is why commodity derivatives trading in India has concentrated on MCX for years.

body.text: Liquidity moats are strong but not unbreakable. BSE relaunched Sensex derivatives in 2023 and won meaningful volumes in index options, helped by a different weekly expiry day that gave traders a new reason to show up. When SEBI limited each exchange to a single weekly index expiry from late 2024, the landscape shifted again. A liquidity network holds only as long as traders have no strong reason to try somewhere else.

children.text: Depositories: A Network Built Through Brokers

CDSL gained ground by becoming the depository of choice for many of the discount brokers that brought millions of new investors into markets. Each broker that connects to CDSL brings its entire client base. Today CDSL holds the majority of demat accounts in India by number, while NSDL holds a larger share of assets by value, reflecting its base of institutional investors. Once a broker has built its systems around one depository, switching is costly, so network effects and switching costs reinforce each other.
When a Network Is Open: The UPI Lesson

UPI is one of the most powerful networks ever built in India, with billions of transactions a month. But the network belongs to the system, run by NPCI, not to any one company. Any UPI app can pay any other UPI user, so a customer on one app gets the full network without joining a rival. The network effect is shared by everyone, which means it protects no one.

Paytm's earlier wallet business had a closed network: you could only pay merchants who accepted Paytm. Interoperable UPI removed that advantage. The lesson for investors is to ask who owns the network. If users can reach everyone through any provider, the network is a public utility, not a company moat.

columns.label: Strong network effects
points: Users cannot easily reach the network through a rival
Users rarely use more than one platform at a time
Value comes from the full network, not a small local part
A clear leader with a widening gap
Hard for a well-funded new entrant to reach critical mass

columns.label: Weak network effects
points: Networks are interoperable, as with UPI
Users and suppliers happily use two or three platforms at once
Value is local, so each city is a new battle
Leadership swings with discounts and incentives
Rivals can buy critical mass with enough spending

children.text: The Multi-Homing Problem

markDefs.definition: When users or suppliers are active on more than one competing platform at the same time. It weakens network effects because no platform has exclusive access to its users.

children.text: Multi-homing

is the biggest threat to marketplace moats. Many restaurants list on both Zomato and Swiggy, and many customers keep both apps and compare. Delivery partners often work across platforms. When both sides multi-home, neither platform fully owns its network, and competition shifts to discounts, speed, and fees. That is why food delivery in India behaves more like a duopoly with occasional price wars than a winner-takes-all market.

body.label: The network moat question
body.value: If a rival matched every feature and offered users ₹500 to join, would the network still hold?
body.context: If users and suppliers would stay because everyone they need is already there, the network is a moat. If they would simply add the rival app, it is not.

body.title: Which Network Is Strongest?
body.question: Which of these businesses has the strongest network effect moat?
options: A UPI payments app with a large user base
A food delivery app in a city where most restaurants and customers also use a rival app
A B2B marketplace where most suppliers in a category list only on it, and buyers search it first because that is where suppliers are
A new stock exchange offering zero transaction fees but with very little trading volume
body.explanation: Option C shows both sides concentrated on one platform with little multi-homing, which is what makes a two-sided network hard to attack. UPI is interoperable, so the network is shared. The food delivery app faces heavy multi-homing. The zero-fee exchange lacks liquidity, which matters more to traders than fees.

cards.definition: The size at which a network becomes useful enough to keep attracting users on its own, without heavy incentives.
A platform connecting two distinct groups, such as buyers and sellers, where each side attracts the other.
A market where traders gather because others are already trading there, giving tighter spreads and faster fills.
Users or suppliers active on several competing platforms at once, which weakens network effects.
When users of different providers can transact with each other, as on UPI. It shares the network effect across all providers.

body.title: The Well-Funded Challenger
body.scenario: A listed online jobs platform has been the market leader in India for over 20 years. Most corporate recruiters subscribe to it, and it has the largest database of CVs. A large global tech company now launches a free jobs product in India, integrated with a professional networking app that many white-collar workers already use daily. It offers recruiters free job postings for the first year.
body.prompt: Will the incumbent's network effect protect it? What evidence would you look for over the next two years?
body.modelAnswer: The incumbent has a real two-sided network: recruiters pay because jobseekers and CVs are there, and jobseekers stay because recruiters are there. But the challenger does not need to build a network from scratch, since it can bring an existing user base from its networking app, and free postings reduce the cost for recruiters to multi-home. The likely outcome is not that the incumbent collapses, but that recruiters use both, which puts pressure on pricing. Evidence to watch: the incumbent's recruiter subscription renewals and pricing; billings growth and any discounting mentioned in concalls; whether jobseekers keep updating CVs on the incumbent; operating margins as it spends to defend its position; and the challenger's share among white-collar versus other hiring segments. If renewals and pricing hold, the network moat is doing its job. If billings slow and discounts rise, multi-homing is eroding it.

body.text: Companies named are used to illustrate concepts from public information and are not investment recommendations. Market positions change; check current exchange, depository, and company disclosures before relying on any detail. The jobs platform scenario is hypothetical.

points: A network effect makes a product more valuable to each user as more users join, creating a self-reinforcing lead
Possible connections grow as n(n−1)/2, so value can grow much faster than user numbers, but relevant connections matter more than the formula
In India, network effects show up in exchanges (liquidity), marketplaces like Naukri and IndiaMART, depositories like CDSL, and local delivery networks
Liquidity moats are strong but can be contested, as BSE's return to index derivatives showed
Interoperable networks like UPI share their value across all providers and protect no single company
Multi-homing is the biggest threat to marketplace moats; ask whether users would stay if a rival paid them to join
